event_overview.title: About US Midterm Elections
event_overview.subject: US Midterm Elections
event_overview.summary: The 2026 U.S. midterm elections are nationwide federal elections held during a presidential term, principally to choose members of Congress. They also coincide with many state and local contests, whose offices, ballot questions, voting procedures and certification rules vary by jurisdiction.

facts.label: Election date
facts.value: Federal law sets congressional general elections for the Tuesday after the first Monday in November in each even-numbered year; in 2026, that date is November 3.

facts.label: Congressional offices
facts.value: All House seats are regularly contested every two years because Representatives are chosen for two-year terms; Senate elections are staggered, with roughly one-third of senators facing election or reelection every two years.

facts.label: Election administration
facts.value: U.S. elections are decentralized: states set many of the rules for conducting and certifying elections, and counties, cities, townships or other local jurisdictions commonly administer voting. Federal law establishes certain nationwide requirements and standards.

facts.label: New congressional terms
facts.value: The members elected to the next Congress begin their terms at noon on January 3, 2027, under the Twentieth Amendment; the statutory election date refers to the Congress beginning the following January 3.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows developments tied to the 2026 midterm campaign and voting period, such as polling, early voting and party messaging; it does not aim to catalog every federal, state or local race, rule, result, recount or certification process.

explore_lenses.title: The transition begins with the 120th Congress
explore_lenses.summary: The current Congress remains in office through January 2, 2027 unless vacancies occur. The next Congress normally convenes at noon on January 3, when the House elects a speaker and swears in members; Senate party conferences organize leadership and committee assignments around the start of the new Congress.

The Senate says party conferences elect leaders with each new Congress and that committee assignments are approved by Senate resolutions; committee seat shares reflect each party’s Senate representation.

The outcome positions Democrats to organize both chambers when the next Congress begins in January 2027, with greater authority over committee operations, legislative scheduling and oversight. The results established Democratic control of both chambers, although final margins remain subject to certification and any recounts.

sections.heading: Iran War’s Electoral Role Disputed
sections.body: The Iran war was among several prominent sources of voter frustration, alongside high prices and concerns about government corruption, AP reported. Vice President JD Vance placed the blame squarely on the conflict, writing that the reason Republicans lost was the war. sections.heading: Congressional Control Takes Effect in January
sections.body: The current Congress ends on Jan. 2, 2027, and a new Congress generally begins at noon the following day. The House elects a speaker at the start of a new Congress, while Senate party conferences select their leaders and the Senate approves committee assignments by resolution. Control would give Democrats greater ability to organize committees and set legislative and oversight priorities, but it would not guarantee enactment: ordinary Senate legislation can require 60 votes for cloture, and overriding a presidential veto requires two-thirds of each chamber.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War refers to the 2026 armed conflict centered on direct hostilities between the United States and Iran, following a wider regional escalation that had included Israeli strikes and Iranian attacks against regional targets. Fighting has been closely tied to the security of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s missile and nuclear capabilities, and negotiations over a ceasefire and longer-term nonproliferation arrangements.

facts.label: Start and setting
facts.value: The major 2026 phase of the conflict began on February 28, 2026, with U.S. and Israeli military action against Iran followed by Iranian attacks affecting states across the Gulf region.

facts.label: Principal parties
facts.value: The direct conflict and ceasefire diplomacy have principally involved the United States and Iran, while Israel, Gulf states and armed groups aligned with Iran have been important regional actors.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Hostilities and their effects have extended beyond Iran to the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, including threats to military facilities and commercial vessels near Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman and Iranian coastal areas.

facts.label: Ceasefire and diplomacy
facts.value: A U.S.-Iran ceasefire was announced on April 7, 2026 and later extended; a June 17 memorandum of understanding provided for cessation of hostilities, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and negotiations toward a broader agreement. The arrangements remained fragile amid subsequent maritime incidents and renewed strikes.

facts.label: Nuclear and legal context
facts.value: The conflict is linked to long-running international concerns over Iran’s nuclear program and safeguards access. The IAEA reported that attacks and Iran’s suspension of cooperation severely reduced its ability to verify nuclear material and facilities; in the United States, Congress has also debated the President’s authority to conduct hostilities against Iran under the War Powers Resolution.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline focuses on late-July 2026 escalation involving threats to Iranian infrastructure, Strait of Hormuz shipping, congressional war-powers action, oil-market effects, Houthi activity and renewed ceasefire talks; it does not provide a complete military, humanitarian, diplomatic or legal history of the conflict before or after that period.

event_overview.title: About Russia-Ukraine War
event_overview.subject: Russia-Ukraine War
event_overview.summary: The Russia-Ukraine War is an interstate conflict rooted in Russia’s 2014 seizure of Crimea and fighting in eastern Ukraine, which expanded into a full-scale Russian armed attack on 24 February 2022. It has involved combat and long-range strikes across Ukraine and, increasingly, attacks affecting Russian territory, alongside major humanitarian, legal, diplomatic and economic consequences.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: In March 2014, the UN General Assembly affirmed Ukraine’s sovereignty, political independence, unity and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, and declared that the 16 March 2014 Crimea referendum could not alter Crimea’s status.

facts.label: Full-scale phase
facts.value: The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission says Russian armed forces launched a full-scale armed attack on Ukraine on 24 February 2022; this is the date generally used for the war’s current large-scale phase.

facts.label: Parties and geography
facts.value: The core belligerents are the Russian Federation and Ukraine. The International Court of Justice’s 16 March 2022 provisional-measures order referred to Russian military operations begun on 24 February 2022 “in the territory of Ukraine.”

facts.label: International legal position
facts.value: On 2 March 2022, the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution ES-11/1, demanding that Russia immediately cease its use of force against Ukraine and withdraw its military forces; the resolution also called for a peaceful resolution through dialogue, negotiations and mediation.

facts.label: Humanitarian impact
facts.value: UN human-rights monitoring has documented extensive civilian harm, displacement and damage to homes, medical and educational facilities, and critical infrastructure; it cautions that verified civilian-casualty totals understate the actual toll where access and verification are limited.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows a limited set of late-July to mid-August 2026 developments, including cross-border strikes, reported casualties and humanitarian findings; it does not provide a comprehensive military, diplomatic or legal history of the war.

event_overview.title: About US Midterm Elections
event_overview.subject: US Midterm Elections
event_overview.summary: The 2026 U.S. midterm elections are nationwide federal elections held during a presidential term, principally to choose members of Congress. They also coincide with many state and local contests, whose offices, ballot questions, voting procedures and certification rules vary by jurisdiction.

facts.label: Election date
facts.value: Federal law sets congressional general elections for the Tuesday after the first Monday in November in each even-numbered year; in 2026, that date is November 3.

facts.label: Congressional offices
facts.value: All House seats are regularly contested every two years because Representatives are chosen for two-year terms; Senate elections are staggered, with roughly one-third of senators facing election or reelection every two years.

facts.label: Election administration
facts.value: U.S. elections are decentralized: states set many of the rules for conducting and certifying elections, and counties, cities, townships or other local jurisdictions commonly administer voting. Federal law establishes certain nationwide requirements and standards.

facts.label: New congressional terms
facts.value: The members elected to the next Congress begin their terms at noon on January 3, 2027, under the Twentieth Amendment; the statutory election date refers to the Congress beginning the following January 3.

event_overview.summary: The Michigan Senate race is the statewide 2026 election for one U.S. Senate seat representing Michigan. Voters are choosing a senator for a six-year term in the November 3, 2026 general election; the official ballot lists Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, Republican nominee Mike Rogers, and candidates from four additional parties.
